Bumping in support of the image-support portion of this.

A current build still exhibits the capability-default problem for custom `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` providers: a model defined only in `opencode.json` with no models.dev entry resolves `capabilities.input` to `["text"]`, so `image/*` parts are dropped before the (already correct) OpenAI-compatible conversion runs. Explicitly setting `modalities.input: ["text", "image"]` per model is the only workaround today.

Direct calls to the same gateway with a base64 `image_url` data URI succeed, so this is purely the client-side default and matches the diagnosis here. Since this PR consolidates the #21627 fix, it looks like the most efficient path to land. Any chance of a review? Happy to test against a self-hosted OpenAI-compatible router if that helps.

Can confirm the root cause here on a current build.

Custom `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` provider defined only in `opencode.json`: the model has no models.dev entry and the gateway's `/v1/models` carries no modality metadata, so `capabilities.input` resolves to `["text"]` and image parts are filtered out before conversion. Setting `modalities.input: ["text", "image"]` per model is a working workaround, which lines up with the diagnosis in this PR.

Note the consolidated version of this change is in #23501, which lists this PR as superseded — probably worth routing review there so the fix isn't split across two threads.

Seeing this on **1.18.30** too.

My setup is a supervisor loop that drives `opencode run` one step at a time and records every invocation, so I have a decent pile of numbers.

**Eleven hangs across three multi-step runs.** Elapsed at the point I killed them:

```
600, 600, 602, 603, 603, 603, 604, 609, 784, 815, 943
```

Eight of eleven land in a nine-second window at 600-609s, and two of those runs were weeks apart on different branches. Zero bytes of output every time, 1.3-1.5% CPU.

The clustering is the part I find suspicious. A lost-wakeup/scheduler bug (#35870) has no clock in it, so it shouldn't pile up on a round number. ~600s looks like something with a 10-minute timeout that fires and then doesn't surface.

One thing about those numbers, though. My supervisor doesn't poll on a fixed interval — I check when a run feels slow. So I can't cleanly claim "the process died at 603s" as against "I noticed at ~603s". The 600-609 tightness across independent runs makes me think it's the former, but I haven't instrumented it properly. I can let one run without killing it and report whether it ever exits on its own, and with what code.

**Same provider as you.** `opencode auth list` shows OpenCode Go as the only credential here, so these are all going through `opencode-go`. Model is `glm-5.3-flash` rather than your `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, so it isn't one model misbehaving.

**On your point 3 (the supervisor-side workaround)** — last-event age is the right clock once a stream has started, but in the zero-event case it means you wait out the full N before you learn anything. I switched to a **first-byte deadline**: my healthy runs put first bytes on stdout within **10-20s**, hung ones never do at all. Paired with a CPU check it's been reliable:

- first bytes inside ~90s → let it run
- zero bytes and ~1.5% CPU → hung, kill and relaunch the same brief

All eleven of mine cleared on an identical re-run, so relaunching costs almost nothing.

Two things to watch with that. Don't set the deadline too low — @nbbdera in #35870 caught a stall that recovered by itself after 44.1s and then ran normally, so anything under 90s will kill runs that were going to work. And CPU% is what stops you killing a healthy-but-quiet run: mine sit near 33% while working, against 1.3-1.5% hung, so pair it with the byte check rather than trusting bytes alone.

**On the watchdog in point 2** — pi solved the same problem and it's worth a look, because the shape they landed on covers the zero-event case that event-keyed watchdogs miss. earendil-works/pi#3020 (closed, shipped) wraps the stream in `withStreamIdleTimeout(source, timeoutMs)`, which **races each `iterator.next()` against a `setTimeout`** and throws `StreamIdleTimeoutError`
when no chunk arrives in the window. Racing the await itself rather than measuring the gap between arrived events is the bit that matters here: the first `next()` gets a deadline too, so a stream that never delivers anything is caught by the same mechanism as one that dies mid-flight. It's off by default (`0`) with 90000ms recommended, and a zero-overhead pass-through when disabled.

On the ~600s number, offered as a guess. The config schema documents `headerTimeout` and `chunkTimeout` at 300000ms each, and 600s is exactly twice that. It's also the OpenAI JS SDK default request timeout. #46692 says those two keys are silently ignored on the v2 `packages/llm` path, so a dropped 5-minute timeout falling through to a 10-minute default would fit what I'm seeing. I haven't read the source, so that's speculation — someone who knows which path `opencode-go` takes could kill or confirm it quickly.

Happy to pull full session logs if the clustering is worth chasing.

Adding a negative result on 1.18.30, plus one thing that has saved me time.

Environment: Fedora 44, kernel 7.1.10, 15 GB RAM with ~8 GB available, 8 cores. Not under memory pressure.

**@kammyrnd's persistent-dir workaround doesn't hold here.** Every one of my runs already uses the same persistent project directory — an ordinary git checkout I work in all day, never a `mktemp -d` — and I still hang on roughly two of three fresh sessions. So on 1.18.30 a warm project dir isn't sufficient, at least for me. That also cuts against box size being the discriminating variable: I'm on a roomy box like @nbbdera's and I hang like @kammyrnd's small one.

**CPU% separates "parked" from "working", which is worth knowing.** A healthy run of mine measures ~33% CPU; a hung one sits at 1.3-1.5% with zero bytes of output. I nearly killed a healthy run on elapsed time alone before I started checking, so this is now the first line of my runbook:

```bash
pgrep -x opencode | while read p; do ps -o pid=,etimes=,%cpu= -p "$p"; done
```

@nbbdera — this doesn't answer the problem you raised, and you were right to raise it. A park that recovers at 44s and a park that never recovers both sit near 0% CPU, so CPU tells you "parked, not working", not "parked forever". It's a different axis. What it does remove is the failure mode where you kill a run that's genuinely chewing on something.

**Where I think my hangs actually belong.** Mine cluster hard at 600-609s (8 of 11 recorded), which doesn't fit a lost wakeup — that has no clock in it — and fits a ~10-minute provider timeout better. `opencode auth list` shows OpenCode Go as my only credential, which is the provider #48675 is about, so I'm probably in that bucket rather than this one and I've put the detail there. The persistent-dir negative result seemed worth leaving here regardless, since it's the workaround this thread is carrying.

One limit on my side: a hung run gives me zero bytes through `tee`, so I can't tell from outside whether a session got created. Next hang I get I'll grab the session log and `ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd/0` (per @nbbdera's #42064 note) and report which one it really was.

I'm having this same issue, with the Student pack. It seems the Student plan (free_educational_quota SKU) reports every Copilot model with model_picker_enabled: false, which opencode maps to enabled: false, so /models showed zero Copilot models despite valid auth and working API access.

Additional data point from OpenCode V2. The native OpenAI path still produced an unbounded stalled turn on the current release.

## Environment

- OpenCode: `2.0.8`, `latest` channel
- Provider/model: `openai/gpt-5.6-sol`, variant `medium`
- OS: macOS, Darwin 24.6.0, arm64
- Terminal: Ghostty, `TERM=xterm-256color`, `COLORTERM=truecolor`
- Shell: `/bin/zsh`
- User-configured plugins: none found
- Session: `ses_f490c3b66ffeSncEFUrgZgaS2h`

## Observed state

The session stopped making progress but remained in the process-local active registry:

```json
{
  "ses_f490c3b66ffeSncEFUrgZgaS2h": {
    "type": "running"
  }
}
```

At the same time:

- `opencode service status` returned a live local service.
- `opencode api get /api/info` returned version `2.0.8` and a live PID.
- The session metadata still reported `outcome: "succeeded"` from its earlier idle boundary.
- The last assistant message was created at `2026-09-19T00:01:42Z` and had no `time.completed`, `finish`, or `error` when inspected more than eight minutes later.
- Its two reasoning parts had completed by `2026-09-19T00:02:01Z`, followed by an empty text part. No finish event arrived.
- The prior assistant turn and all its tool calls had completed.
- Session inbox, permission requests, and running shell commands were empty.
- The normal log had no error, retry, or timeout entry for this session.

This looks consistent with the native `packages/llm` stream path not applying a chunk timeout. It is also a real-release confirmation for the failure that #49229 is intended to fix.

Your two reconciliations here are the clearest evidence I have seen that subagent spend is invisible in the UI: two independent methods landing at 42% and 84%.

I have been standardising how delegation boundaries get counted, and your case is the exact failure mode I am trying to pin down: child spend that never rolls up to the parent. The draft checks are three vectors in `conformance/vectors/delegation-001-003.json` (DELEGATION-001 is the no-flattening one).

Would you read those three and tell me whether DELEGATION-001 actually captures your case, or whether the real invariant is narrower than what I wrote?

Useful feedback would be a field the vectors are missing, a case they classify wrongly, or the shape of your two reconciliation queries if you are willing to share them.

Closing in favour of #49875.

While wiring this up on the AIMS side I found that `opencode://new-session` doesn't work at all on a current install, so the aliases this PR adds are spellings for a mechanism that never fires.

The handler navigates to `/${slug}/session`, which only matches in the legacy shell (`/:dir` has a `/session/:id?` child). Under the new layout designs the only `/:dir/…` route requires an `:id`, so the href matches nothing — the project opens, the window comes forward, and the prompt is silently dropped. With `newLayoutDesignsDefault` true and the old-interface sunset passed, that's everyone.

#49875 fixes that by creating a draft and navigating to `/new-session?draftId=…` under the new layout. Once a new-session link actually works, the short form is worth revisiting on its own merits — but it shouldn't ride along with the fix.

I have a working implementation of the second option mentioned above (preserve the detected original encoding on write), and would like to offer it as a complement to #45925.

#45925 protects the core (v2) tools by rejecting non-UTF-8 files — the right minimal fix there. This covers the v1 tools in `packages/opencode` (edit / write / read / apply_patch + the patch engine), which currently still have the same bug, and goes one step further: instead of refusing to touch non-UTF-8 files, it detects the encoding per read (BOM → UTF-8 validity → configurable fallback) and writes back in the same encoding, so legacy files stay editable:

- New config `file_encoding` (default `"utf-8"` → default behavior unchanged), e.g. `"gbk"`, `"shift_jis"`
- Files with BOM (UTF-8 / UTF-16LE / UTF-16BE) work without any configuration
- Other encodings via lazily-imported `iconv-lite` (zero cost on the UTF-8 path)
- Byte-level round-trip tests: GBK edit/write/read, UTF-16 BOM, UTF-8 BOM preserved, file left byte-identical when an edit does not match

Happy to scope it down or rebase however maintainers prefer (e.g. land after #45925). Opening a PR referencing this issue.

Three details not covered here or in #49412 / #44028. The first matters most, because the obvious workaround destroys data.

### Resetting the KV marker destroys the event log

Deleting `kv.migration.v1-v2` to force a re-run is not safe. From a cleared state the importer deletes the **entire** `event` table before it copies anything.

Where V1 kept running after the marker was set, every row in `event` belongs to the sessions that are still missing: V1 persists a durable event per message and part, while V2's CLI path persists none. Resetting the marker therefore wipes the event log of exactly the sessions being recovered.

### `event_sequence` must not be lowered to the projection watermark

The importer upserts `event_sequence.seq` to `transformSession`'s watermark, which is only safe because it has already emptied `event`.

For an aggregate whose events survive, `event` has a unique index on `(aggregate_id, seq)` and new events publish at `latest + 1`, so lowering the sequence makes the next publish collide with an existing row. Keeping the original value avoids this; the only cost is a gap in `session_message.seq`, harmless because the projector and the bus order by seq rather than assume contiguity. An incremental importer would need to handle this rather than reuse the current upsert.

### The status endpoint reports `completed` while sessions are missing

`GET /api/experimental/migration/v1` answers from the KV marker alone and never compares `session` against `session_v2`, so anything built on it reports a healthy migration. Returning `required` whenever the difference is non-empty would be a cheap fix.

### Suggested direction

Drive the import from the set difference rather than a completion marker, drop the unconditional `event` wipe, and leave `event_sequence` alone for aggregates that still have events. That also makes the job re-entrant, which the mixed V1/V2 window requires.

### Workaround

`transformSession` from `@opencode/core/database/v1-migration.bun` is exported as a pure function, so the missing sessions can be recovered out-of-band: copy the set difference into `session_v2` and rebuild `session_message` from `message` and `part` through it, leaving `event`, `event_sequence` and the marker untouched. Run under bun, since the node condition resolves to a noop build. Snapshot with `.backup` and stop the service before writing.

### Environment

- opencode 2.0.8, installed with the official `curl` install script
- Fedora Linux 44, x86_64

I reproduced this on OpenCode Desktop 2.0.8 (Windows, stable) with bundled CLI 2.0.8, running on WSL 2.9.12.0 (kernel 6.18.40.1-1).
The test distro is Ubuntu with `/usr/bin/zsh` as its default shell, and the issue also reproduces with bash configured as the default shell.
Inside WSL, `~/.opencode/bin/opencode` reports `opencode v2.0.8`, matching the desktop version.

Settings → Ubuntu displays **Install OpenCode**, and the desktop log records:

```
wsl sidecar failed to start { id: 'wsl:Ubuntu', distro: 'Ubuntu', message: 'OpenCode is not installed in Ubuntu' }
```

Discovery fails before the version check runs, so this failure is not a version gate.

### Minimal reproduction

The issue reproduces on Windows using PowerShell 7.6.6 with `$PSNativeCommandArgumentPassing = Windows`:

```powershell
$mini = 'cli="x"' + [char]10 + 'echo "cli=$cli"'
& wsl.exe -d Ubuntu --     sh -lc $mini   # -> cli=
& wsl.exe -d Ubuntu --exec sh -lc $mini   # -> cli=x
```

When called with `--`, WSL runs the argument through the distro's default Linux shell.
That outer shell expands `$cli` before the target `sh` process executes.
The script remains a single argument, but its contents change.
A NUL-preserving `/proc/self/cmdline` capture shows this expansion:

```
--:     ["sh", "-lc", "base64 </proc/self/cmdline\ncli=\"x\"\necho \"cli=\""]
--exec: ["sh", "-lc", "base64 </proc/self/cmdline\ncli=\"x\"\necho \"cli=$cli\""]
```

### Application mapping

- `RemoteCli.discoverScript()` (via `runWslSh`) arrives with `$cli` expanded to empty, so `resolveWslCli()` returns empty and `spawnWslSidecar` reports not installed.
- `RemoteCli.versionScript()` survives both forms because it uses a quoted absolute path with no assignment-dependent interpolation.
- `spawnWslSidecar` sends its script over stdin (`bash -se`); that payload is unaffected, but it never runs because discovery fails first.
- The install verification contains `$()`, so it is exposed to the same pre-expansion.
  Harmless probes confirm the premature substitution; no installer was run.

### Verification of the fix

Probes against WSL 2.9.12.0 show the behavior difference between `--` and `--exec`:

```
                            --                    --exec
discover script             (empty)               /home/<user>/.opencode/bin/opencode
cli="x" / echo "cli=$cli"   cli=                  cli=x
version script              opencode v2.0.8       opencode v2.0.8
/bin/true                   exit 0                exit 0
bash -se over stdin         correct               correct
--user <user>               n/a                   correct identity and $HOME
```

This verifies the discovery fix in PR #48796 (`wslArgs()` changing from `--` to `--exec`).
This test is not an end-to-end Desktop startup test because the probes used PowerShell/.NET argument lists.
A call-site audit found no regressions: explicit `sh -lc`/`bash -lc` calls still interpret their own scripts, and only the unwanted outer-shell pass is removed.
One caveat: bypassing the default shell also bypasses its startup-file environment changes, so a PATH/environment smoke test is worthwhile.

Its inline-and-quote workaround differs from the `--exec` fix verified here; that case did not involve argument splitting, and inline quoting is not automatically sufficient for these runtime-dependent scripts.
